title: Settings in an inventory tool
metaTitle: Inventory settings are a small cabinet
excerpt: Inventory settings are a cabinet. The person on the floor changes zone, text size, and sound. Cost method and admin belong buried, or the cabinet becomes a second product.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall, a few things hung where you can reach them.
caption: Only the things you reach for belong at the front of the cabinet. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should inventory settings show the floor first?
faqs.answer: Show the zone or warehouse they are working, the text size, and whether the scanner beeps. Those change during a shift. Costing method, tax, user admin, and integrations belong in an office cabinet the floor login cannot open. A shared settings page becomes a second product the floor must learn and fear.

faqs.question: Should scanner sound live in settings?
faqs.answer: The default can live in settings, and the task screen should still show a visible confirmation that does not depend on sound, because some aisles are loud and some people mute the device. If they change the sound mid-shift, they should not lose the line they were counting. Settings are an errand, and the count is the job.

faqs.question: How do office settings stay off the floor device?
faqs.answer: Use a different session, not a longer scroll: floor login sees zone, display, and sound, and lead or office login sees costing, users, and integrations. Hiding a row is better than disabling it. A disabled cost method on a shared phone will get tapped all shift.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Inventory tool settings UX is a cabinet, not a second product. The person on the floor changes a few things during a shift: the zone they are standing in, the size of the type, and whether the scanner makes a sound. Group those. Bury the rest. Cost method does not belong between them and the next bin.

The office changes different things, sitting down: who can adjust, how value is calculated, which location is the system of record. That cabinet can be larger. It should not be the same screen, on the same login, as the floor's. One shared page is how a picker opens "valuation method" by mistake.

## What the floor changes often

Zone or warehouse comes first. Shifts move. A person who counted receiving in the morning may pick in another aisle after lunch. The current zone should be visible in the task header and editable here. Changing it should say what happens to an unconfirmed line. Do not silently abandon a count because they fixed their zone.

Type size comes next. Arm's length, glare, and tired eyes are the use case. Offer a simple larger-text control and honor the operating system size as the default. If your layout breaks when the type grows, the layout is not done. The floor will keep the size they can read, and your perfect density will lose.

Sound and haptics come third. Some aisles allow a beep. Some do not. A switch for scan sound, with the visible check still mandatory, is the whole design. Do not bury the beep inside a theme called "experience." They will not find it, and they will tape over the speaker.

Language belongs here if the crew is mixed. Set it per device or per person, and keep item names in the language printed on the carton even if the chrome changes. Translating the bin label away from the paint on the rack is a mistake. The rack is the source of truth for the word they search.

Offline behavior, if they can choose it, is a floor setting. "Keep counting when the network drops" should be on by default if the device can store lines. If you let them turn it off, say the consequence in the switch's sentence. A vague "sync mode" label is office language.

Jakob Nielsen noted that people leave pages quickly and read little of the text when the point is buried. A settings screen is under that pressure even in a quieter corner of the warehouse. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a reason to show Zone, Text, and Sound as sentences at the top, not as a grid of identical gears.

## What to bury, and from whom

Cost method, tax, and account codes are office settings. Hide them from the floor login. A disabled row is still an invitation, and on a shared device it will be tapped with a glove until someone files a bug.

User admin is a lead's job. Who can adjust, who can count which zone. It lives in the office cabinet. The floor cabinet can show "You are signed in as Sam" and a way to switch user. It should not list every employee and their rights.

Integrations, barcodes label templates for the office printer, and API keys are not shift settings. They change a few times in a year. Put them behind the office login, at the end of that cabinet, with plain warnings. The floor should not scroll past a webhook to reach text size.

Delete item, merge duplicates, and bulk edit are destructive office tools. They do not belong on a phone that lives in a holster. If a lead must do them on the floor, put them in the lead session behind an explicit destructive confirmation that names the item. Never behind a swipe the floor uses to skip a line.

Notification settings for the office, such as low-stock emails, are not the picker's. Do not ask the floor to manage the office's inbox. If the picker needs one alert, "this bin is on hold," it belongs on the bin, not in a notification matrix.

## The cabinet must not eat the count

Opening settings is an errand in the middle of a line. The unconfirmed quantity stays. Returning lands on the same line. If changing zone cannot keep the line, ask before you discard it. The same rule as search. The same rule, because it is the same risk: a double count or a lost one.

Do not require a settings tour at the start of every shift. Remember the last zone and the last text size on that login. Ask them to confirm the zone in one tap if the shift start matters. One tap is not a wizard. A wizard that explains modules is a tour. Skip it.

Write switches as sentences. "Beep when a scan matches." "Use larger type." A switch named Audio next to a switch named Display next to a switch named Data is a puzzle. They will flip the wrong one and notice two aisles later.

Save immediately for switches. Say "Saved" in text, not only by motion. For the zone, which has consequences, confirm if a count is open, then save, then show the new zone in the header before they walk. The header is the proof. A checkmark inside settings is not enough, because they leave settings.

## One device, two cabinets

Supervisors often grab the nearest phone. If that phone can become a lead session, the switch should be obvious and reversible. "Viewing as floor" and "Viewing as lead" in the header prevents a supervisor from thinking the floor sees the adjustment tools they see.

Build the floor cabinet with so few rows that a stranger can read it aloud in half a minute. That constraint is the design. If you need a sixth row, you are probably putting an office job on the floor. Move the job.

The office cabinet can group Locations, People, Valuation, and Connections. Full sentences still help. The office user is less hurried and more dangerous, because their toggles change the ledger. Destructive groups go last, named by the damage, not by "Advanced." Advanced is where teams hide the controls that scare them. Scary controls need daylight and a specific label.

Do not clone a consumer app's settings. Profile photos, themes, and social links are noise in a warehouse tool. A dark background that reduces glare is a display setting, and it is legitimate. A theme shop is not.


## What a shift start is allowed to ask

At the start of a shift, one question is enough: which zone. Remember the last answer and let them confirm it with a tap. Do not ask them to re-accept notifications, re-pick a theme, or read a changelog. A changelog is an office document. The floor needs the first bin, and every extra question is a reason to leave the device on the desk and take a paper list.

If the device was used by someone else, the shift start is also the user switch. Show the previous name and require a deliberate change. A phone that silently stays on the last person will attribute a count to the wrong name, and your permissions will be blamed for a handoff problem. The cabinet can contain the switch. The task header has to show the result, in the same name the supervisor uses on the roster.

Battery and offline belong in one sentence if they change the count. Say whether lines stay on the device with no network, and do not claim they survive a dead battery unless a reboot proved it. Put that sentence on the task, not only in the cabinet. Settings are where they change the behavior. The task is where they decide to trust it. If the device is too low to finish an aisle, say so before they walk away from the charger, not as a failure on the last bin when the unsent lines die with the phone.
## Review a shift change

Sign in as the floor. Open settings from an unconfirmed line. Change text size. Go back. The quantity should still be there, and the type should actually be larger on the item name. Change zone with a quantity typed. The product should ask before it drops the line.

Sign in as the office on a desk. You should see valuation and people. Sign in as the floor on the phone. You should not. If both logins share one long page, split them before you add another toggle.

The next first screen in this set is a different room again. A client who was promised a file does not need a zone switch. They need the file. That piece is [the first screen of a client portal](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-client-portal). Leave the warehouse cabinet here.

If the floor cabinet and the count screen should be designed as one tool, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Settings that feel like a second product will be skipped, and the skipped switch will be the one that made the type readable.
